From: A pleural cavity deep in Dr. Michael McDuffy’s left lung crackled menacingly. He exchanged a glance with Dr. Marjorie “Maya” Tanaka, nodding as their fingers met in a silent pact. "Perfect," McDuffy said, before coughing up a globule of thick green sputum onto the sterile bedside tray. He barked out a drenched gag. "*Christo*." 
"I think the pathologist found it on autopsy," Maya said flatly.
"Yeah," McDuffy snarked, his eyes scandalized. He mocked her with a morbid smile. "If only your patients were interesting, like some poor soul who *gagged* at the sight of it. Now *that* would be dreadful!" 
"You’re the on-call butler for this shitty ward, Mon, not the full-time chief pathology gig!" Maya said, leaning back. "Now get to diagnosing or I’ll stomp out before the filmmakers of *Mozart in the Invisible Joke* squander this day.”
McDuffy looked around the sterile gloom of the ICU, full of muffled beeps. The mottled wall lights cast eerie shadows over the chemotherapies and the IV lines. He spotted one of the monitors and laid a gloved hand on one of the sensors. "It's startling how still these patients can be," he said, "especially after a flash of life and then...none. Like they just fell silent."
Maya snorted. "So *bad pilot* or runaway bus?" she asked, in the Mancunian accent that made her sound like she rubbed her butt with a broom handle.
His jaw twisted. "Both," McDuffy said in a voice strict as a schoolteacher. "Terrible way to go."
He wandered over to another bed and leaned against a hook of IV tubes. As he traced the network of lines to a hidden jugular, a shadow slipped past behind a curtain.
Maya peered at him. "Don’t worry, Mon. My bed solitude is even *better* than yours. And the admission is *inherently* better than yours." She fluffed up her hairstreaked hair as if she used hairspray usually reserved for cosplay. "And I will get you a new, shiny iPad next Tuesday."
McDuffy, struck suddenly by the line, deadpanned, "You'd better do better than that or you'll die of boredom!"
Suddenly, Maya’s gaze slid over to a small plastic paternity clock, glowing in the shadows near the drone of an oxygen tank.
Maya’s mouth curled even tighter, even as she concealed a sigh. "He drilled you for three hours but still said the wrong information. I guess we both know how much potential that leaves."
McDuffy snorted. "Three hours!?" he huffed, eyes bugging in feigned horror. “I’ve been here two whole minutes! And if you stopped me now I could swear they’d expel me entirely! The way you both wait for those two minutes, then stand there with your eyes … ah there, that’s enough, no yabba dabba doo with the navel gazing. Or what am I supposed to do when the bed shakes with the conscientious sleep timer something, during the post-lunch dia.."
Maya, who had become a statue of judgmental silence, whipped her brows up in disapproval. “Mon in the ICU, how utterly incredible that you apparently never before clued into the fact that at one point or another, your patients can even – I don’t know – BEHAVE?"
McDuffy darted to the nearest window seat, his body wriggling as he took another therapist’s wing. When he pulled out a battered old tablet, he glanced over his shoulder, flashed her a sheepish lop. "I was distracted. How DARE you say I don't remember things! I can see what 's happening even while I'm here!" He jabbed a finger at the tablet, which he slid across the table, and to the amazed silence of the empty room, a vid popped up showing snippets from Maya’s last "assignment".

Maya watched, bemused, as he poked the screen. "Go ahead, Mon. Whatever you want."
Montrose looked up in confusion, studying her for a hesitant moment. "Well, I didn't think you'd be so respectful. I just wanted to be sure. Have I done something wrong for... never mind," he sighed. "I have a tendency to overdo things – you can, after all, mistake friendship for something you don’t quite understand. I'd never subject you to such hardship when I could have been on-love... ‘… wouldn't define me… I'd rather do this on my own.’ I don’t know why. I used to think…" he gave a sigh of silent resignation, brushing his brow with a hand. "I just know something tells me it would be best to just try to stay out of everyone’s way for now. I don’t want to have a reason to regret it one day." He hesitated before adding. "And if it’s so... frustrating I know it can't be easy. The others are there. Maybe it matters, I dunno. But if you need to work with a capable friend here, on my terms I’ll do my best — I just hope even if I have to love you for what I know instead of what I want right now. I think I can only pretend right now. Just that…” He shrugged, looking away, then with a weak smile, put his phone away. “I mean, I knew it could have all gone unread, that I read something kind of silly, but I figured I better… sorry if it’s too tired or too… nothing? You saw it sent from something that only you can see — well, or at least only if it’s in quotes," he flitted his hands and added, and the curtains waved like frosted feathers in the window. "If any of that makes sense. Speaking of dreams and real life, what time is it? I hate being here late. We should have already arrived back at the farm. Do they know if Alphonso is safe?" 

Maya furrowed her brows, quietly bewildered and wide-eyed. "You keep sending me footage of what you're seeing from across the world, Mon?" she asked, shaking her head slowly with a small sigh. "Why are we looking for trouble right now, anyway?" 
Mon looked straight ahead, his gaze riveted not on the video playing on the tablet, but across the sterile room, as if transfixed by a distant, unyielding force. He murmured, "Maybe we're not in the best timeline after all." 

With a small, slow exhale, he reached for Maya's hand, not looking at her eyes but resting his fingers lightly on the back of her wrist, as if she were still there even as her own features began to cycle with conflicting imagery. "I'm here. You're not alone," he said, voice barely more than a breath over the white noise of machines, and suddenly the recording was cut off.

Maya’s eyes widened in silent alarm, and her hand clenched the nurse call bell. The panic in her voice echoed across the hall as she shouted, “MEDIC! NOW!” The alarm blared, cutting through the silence like a knife.

McDuffy, leaving only a faint residue of himself as an image on the monitor, had slipped away—leaving behind him only the twisted fragments of a nightmare he’d dreamed onto the bed.
